ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethics declaration-All the study methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations of the institutional review board (IRB) of the University of Pittsburgh and were approved by the IRB.
The University of Pittsburgh institutional review board approved this study, and all participants provided written consent or assent for their participation.

Bereaved young adults and adolescents aged 7-29 years old who lost a biological parent in the past year due to sudden death such as suicide, accident or natural death (within 24 hours of the initial incident) were recruited to a longitudinal study examining the effect of bereavement on children's mental health.

All participants were identified via medical examiner reports or newspaper advertisements, with recruitment methods and specific reasons of death described previously (Melhem et al., 2007). 71% of those eligible to study were consented to participate.
table.formatted: All participants were identified via medical examiner reports or newspaper advertisements, with recruitment methods and specific reasons of death described previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Melhem et al., 2007)</ref>. 71% of those eligible to study were consented to participate.

table.text: The University of Pittsburgh institutional review board approved this study, and all participants provided written consent or assent for their participation.

Three-hundred and eighty participants completed baseline assessments of anger and physical aggression and were included in the analysis, 47 were excluded from the analysis due to missing data on anger and physical aggression or had experienced another loss during the study.
Personality disorders in adult participants were assessed with the Structured Interview for DSM-IV Personality Disorders.
Surviving caregivers of bereaved participants were more likely to be female, demonstrated poorer functioning, and had higher rates of depression, bipolar disorder, and anxiety disorders.

Compared with the proband parents of non-bereaved participants, deceased parents of bereaved participants were less likely to be White and had higher rates of depression, bipolar disorder, alcohol or substance use disorders, and personality disorders.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Ethics declaration-All the study methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations of the institutional review board (IRB) of the University of Pittsburgh and were approved by the IRB.

The sudden death of a parent is one of the most profound and disruptive stressors a young individual can experience, often triggering acute and enduring turmoil in mental health, family functioning, and developmental adaptation .

Given that more than 2.9 million children under the age of 18 have experienced parental loss in the United States , research has increasingly focused on identifying its psychological and behavioral consequences.

Parentally bereaved youth are at increased risk for depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, substance use, functional impairment, and health-risk behaviors, with some difficulties persisting into adulthood .

However, although sadness and yearning are commonly recognized manifestations of grief , anger and physical aggression may also represent important, yet relatively understudied, responses to parental loss.
14 5 2,3,68 (American Psychiatric Association, Edition, 2013)
Parental death may increase vulnerability to anger and physical aggression by disrupting the family and social resources that support emotion regulation .
Bereavement can impair the functioning of the surviving caregiver, and reduce family cohesion and parental monitoring .
These disruptions may limit opportunities for youth to process the loss and regulate intense emotions, such as anger.
Indeed, longitudinal research provides evidence that parental bereavement may increase vulnerability to aggressive and other externalizing behaviors.
One study found that parental death before age 16 was associated with greater prevalence of delinquent behavior, particularly when the death occurred during adolescence .
Similarly, another study found that parentally bereaved male and female adolescents exhibited greater delinquency and fighting than their nonbereaved counterparts .
Although most group differences diminished over seven years, bereaved females continued to report greater involvement in fighting .
Among maltreated youth, bereavement prospectively predicted increased externalizing problems from early to middle adolescence.
Research using criminal records has similarly linked childhood parental death with later violent behaviors.
Parental loss was associated with approximately twice the risk of violent criminal violent behaviors among males followed from adolescence into adulthood .
Large population-based registry studies also found elevated risks of violent criminal convictions following parental death, including assault, robbery, weapon-related offenses, threats, and arson .

Risks were generally greater following external, unnatural, or suicidal parental deaths, although patterns differed according to the sex of the offspring and the deceased parent, and the age of the child at the time of loss.

These studies provide evidence of an association between parental death and serious externalized violence, however, their reliance on criminal convictions captures only the most severe behavioral outcomes and offers limited information about the emotional expressions of anger and more subtle physical aggression.
Findings involving less severe forms of aggression and health-risk behavior have been more limited.

At approximately 9 months after parental death, found no statistically significant differences between bereaved and nonbereaved youth in individual violence-related behaviors, including physical fighting and weapon carrying.

However, when the same cohort was followed longitudinally, bereaved youth demonstrated persistently higher levels of health-risk behaviors across three years than nonbereaved controls, even after accounting for pre-loss and post-loss risk factors .
In addition, suicide-bereaved children and adolescents have reported greater anger and more behavioral problems than youth bereaved by other causes of parental death .
These findings suggest that the behavioral consequences of bereavement may not be fully evident at one cross-sectional assessment and may become clearer when trajectories are examined prospectively.
Importantly, the occurrence of parental death alone may not fully explain these outcomes.
The severity of grief reactions may be more directly related to anger and aggression than bereavement status itself.

Among persistently delinquent adolescents, bereavement-related distress predicted externalizing symptoms, particularly among boys, even after accounting for PTSD, maltreatment, and psychopathy-spectrum traits .
Nevertheless, this study involved a small sample of incarcerated youth and examined broad externalizing syndromes rather than anger and physical aggression separately.

More recent longitudinal evidence from homicidally bereaved adults demonstrated reciprocal associations between prolonged grief symptoms and state anger across four assessments, with prolonged grief symptoms predicting subsequent anger more strongly than anger predicted subsequent prolonged grief symptoms .

However, this study's focus on adults exposed to violent loss limits its generalizability to parentally bereaved youth and does not clarify whether grief-related anger translates into overt physical aggression.
Thus, the current study aims to (1) Examine whether bereavement and prolonged grief are related to anger and physical aggression, cross-sectionally and longitudinally.
We hypothesize that bereavement and prolonged grief will be associated with higher anger and physical aggression both cross-sectionally and longitudinally.

Bereaved young adults and adolescents aged 7-29 years old who lost a biological parent in the past year due to sudden death such as suicide, accident or natural death (within 24 hours of the initial incident) were recruited to a longitudinal study examining the effect of bereavement on children's mental health.
The study was conducted from August 9, 2002 through December 31, 2013.

All participants were identified via medical examiner reports or newspaper advertisements, with recruitment methods and specific reasons of death described previously (Melhem et al., 2007). 71% of those eligible to study were consented to participate.

text.text: The University of Pittsburgh institutional review board approved this study, and all participants provided written consent or assent for their participation.
Baseline assessment occurred on average, around 9 months after parents' death, while follow-ups occurred at 21, 33, 62, and 84 months, on average, after death.

Three-hundred and eighty participants completed baseline assessments of anger and physical aggression and were included in the analysis, 47 were excluded from the analysis due to missing data on anger and physical aggression or had experienced another loss during the study.
Compared with excluded participants, those included in the analyses were less likely to be bereaved, non-White, or have a history of ADHD.
They also exhibited lower posttraumatic stress symptoms and higher global functioning.
Their caregivers were less likely to be non-White and had higher global functioning.
No significant differences were found in aggression or violence-related behaviors (Supplementary Table 1).
text.formatted: No significant differences were found in aggression or violence-related behaviors (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Of the sample included in the analysis, 206 were parentally bereaved and 174 were frequency-matched non-bereaved controls (Total N=380).
Of the 206 parentally bereaved participants, 66 had parents who died by suicide, 49 by accident and 91 by natural death.
Of the 380 participants included in the analysis, 299 (78.6%) were retained in the study and had complete data in all 4 follow-ups assessments.

Compared with participants who were not retained, those retained in the study were less likely to be bereaved and reported lower aggression, violencerelated behaviors, and suicidal ideation, as well as lower rates of substance use disorders, better functioning, and higher family cohesion.
Retained participants and their caregivers were more likely to be White, and their caregivers demonstrated better functioning and lower rates of bipolar disorder and PTSD.
Their parents also had lower rates of bipolar and personality disorders (Supplementary Table 2).
text.formatted: Their parents also had lower rates of bipolar and personality disorders (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Baseline and follow-up assessments were conducted through in person interviews by clinically certified study clinicians for participants and their surviving caregivers separately.
Sociodemographic characteristics such as age, gender, race and socioeconomic status assessed by the Hollingshead's scale were measured at baseline for both participants and their surviving caregiver.
Aggression and violence-related behaviors were assessed using the Aggression Questionnaire and the Youth Risk Behavior Questionnaire .
The Aggression Questionnaire consists of 29 items assessing four domains: physical aggression, verbal aggression, anger, hostility and indirect.
Items are rated on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (extremely uncharacteristic of me) to 5 (extremely characteristic of me), with higher scores indicating greater aggression.

The Youth Risk Behavior (YRB) Questionnaire is an adaptation of the Youth Risk Behavior Survey , which assesses health-risk behaviors prioritized for surveillance by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, including behaviors contributing to unintentional injury and violence.

The current study included two violence-related behaviors: carrying a weapon, including a gun, knife, or club, during the past 30 days (Item 6) and involvement in a physical fight during the past 12 months (Item 11).
Items were rated using frequency-based response options ranging from 0 (0 times) to 4 (6 or more times).

Items assessing sexual violence were not included in the analysis since they were outside the primary focus of the study on physical aggression, whereas other violence-related items assessed more specific aspects of weapon carrying and physical fighting already captured by the selected items.
Prolonged grief.
At the time the study was initiated, prolonged grief reactions were referred to as "complicated grief," a term now commonly described as "prolonged grief" .

Prolonged grief for surviving caregiver and participants aged 18 years and above was measured by the 19-item inventory for complicated grief (ICG) , with a clinical threshold of 25 or higher indicating clinical prolonged grief .

The 28-item Inventory for Complicated Grief-Revised for Children (ICG-RC) was used to assess prolonged grief in participants aged 18 years and under, with a clinical threshold of 68 or higher indicating clinical prolonged grief symptoms.
Standardized scores of both inventories were used to reflect the severity of prolonged grief symptoms in both child and adult participants.
Clinical prolonged grief was also used as a binary outcome using cut-off scores for both inventories.

Circumstances of exposure to death (CED) a semi-structured interview was used to assess experiences surrounding the death, reflecting the participant's experience at and following the death of the parent .

Psychiatric disorders prior to the death were assessed using the Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age Children-Present and Lifetime Version and the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID) Axis I Disorders for children and adult participants, and their surviving caregiver, respectively.
This was conducted as a retrospective report on psychopathology prior to the death.
A psychological autopsy was also used to assess the deceased parents' lifetime history of psychiatric disorders .
Personality disorders in adult participants were assessed with the Structured Interview for DSM-IV Personality Disorders.
General functioning for participants aged under 18 years was assessed using the Children's Global Assessment Scale (CGAS) , indicating functioning at home and school.
The Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF) was used for those who are older than 18 years old and their surviving caregiver .
High interrater reliability was maintained for the assessment of psychiatric diagnoses (kappa=0.74-0.85; N=107) and impairment (intraclass correlation= 0.92, 95% CI=0.90, 0.93; N=734) .

Clinical symptoms, including depression, anxiety, posttraumatic stress, suicidal ideation severity, and negative coping, were assessed using the Beck Depression Inventory , Beck Anxiety Inventory , Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Symptom Scale-Interview (PSSI-I) , Suicidal Ideation Questionnaire-Junior (SIQ-JR) , and Ways of Coping Questionnaire , respectively.

Protective factors, including self-esteem, social support, and family cohesion, were assessed using the Weinberger Adjustment Inventory self-esteem subscale , Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support , and Family Adaptability and Cohesion Evaluation Scales-II , respectively.
Stressors, including physical and sexual abuse were measured by the post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) section of the psychiatric interview and the Abuse Dimensional Inventory .
Negative life events were assessed using the Life Events Checklist for participants under 18 years old and the shortened Social Readjustment Rating Scale for participants aged 18 years and older.
All statistical analysis were conducted using R program .

Independent samples t-test and Chi-square test were used to examine differences in sociodemographic and clinical characteristics of the participants, surviving caregiver and deceased parent between those bereaved vs. non-bereaved, and the type of parent's death among bereaved participants.

For data reduction, we conducted an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) using baseline data for the Aggression questionnaire and the weapon carrying and physical fighting items from the YRB questionnaire.
Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin and Bartlett's tests supported factorability.
Varimax rotation was applied, and parallel analysis indicated two-factor-solution: Factor 1, reflected anger, and included hostility, indirect aggression, verbal aggression and anger.
Factor 2, reflected physical aggression, included physical aggression, physical fighting, and weapon carrying; Supplementary Table 3).

Measurement invariance was not consistently supported across the configural, metric, scalar, and residual models based on all examined fit indices (Supplementary Table 4).

text.text: To examine whether bereavement and prolonged grief were associated with higher levels of anger and physical aggression at baseline, separate linear regression models were conducted for anger (Factor 1) and physical aggression (Factor 2).
In the full sample, bereavement was examined as the primary predictor of each outcome.
Prolonged grief severity was examined separately within the bereaved sample only.
Models were adjusted for age, sex, race, and socioeconomic status.

Additional covariates were entered hierarchically in blocks reflecting their temporal and clinical order: (1) participants' history of psychiatric disorders; (2) surviving caregivers' history of psychopathology and clinical functioning; (3) deceased parents' history of psychopathology; (4) experiences surrounding the death; and (5) participants' and surviving caregivers' post-loss clinical characteristics.
Variables that were not applicable to a given analytic sample were excluded.
Multicollinearity was examined within and across blocks.
Models were subsequently refined using backward elimination using alpha level of >.05.

text.text: Within the bereaved sample, additional linear regression models examined whether the type of parental death was cross-sectionally associated with each outcome.

To examine whether bereavement and prolonged grief were associated with changes in anger and physical aggression over time, longitudinal associations were examined using separate linear mixed-effects regression models for each outcome.

Models included bereavement status, time, and the bereavement-by-time interaction to determine whether bereaved and non-bereaved participants differed in changes in anger and physical aggression over time.
The models included repeated observations nested within participants and accounted for the clustering of participants within the same family.
Days since baseline was used as the measure of time in these models.

Within the bereaved sample, separate models included prolonged grief severity, time, and the prolonged-grief-by-time interaction to examine whether grief severity was associated with changes in each outcome overtime.
Parental death type and its interaction with time were similarly examined in separate models within the bereaved sample.
Covariates were entered and refined using the same hierarchical and backward-elimination procedures applied in the crosssectional analyses.

text.text: To our knowledge, this is one of the first studies to longitudinally examine the associations of prolonged grief with anger and physical aggression among parentally bereaved youth.
Bereavement alone was not associated with anger or physical aggression after adjustment for sociodemographic and clinical factors, either cross-sectionally or longitudinally.
In contrast, clinical prolonged grief was associated with higher anger at baseline and increasing anger over time, but not with physical aggression.
In addition, physical aggression increased more steeply over time among youth bereaved by sudden natural death than among those bereaved by suicide.

Our finding that bereavement was not independently associated with anger or physical aggression after adjustment for covariates suggests that parental loss alone may not be sufficient to explain these outcomes.

This aligns with prior findings from the same cohort showing no significant cross-sectional differences between bereaved and non-bereaved youth in specific violence-related behaviors, including physical fighting and weapon carrying .
However, it contrasts with research linking parental bereavement to delinquency, fighting, externalizing behaviors, and violent criminality .

These discrepancies may reflect differences in the outcomes examined, as previous studies often assessed broad health-risk behaviors, delinquency, or criminal convictions rather than examining anger and physical aggression separately.

Although bereaved youth from this cohort previously demonstrated persistently higher overall health-risk behaviors (including unsafe driving and substance use) across three years , the current findings indicate that changes in physical aggression over time did not differ significantly between bereaved and non-bereaved participants.

Our findings also indicate that bereaved youth with clinical prolonged grief exhibited higher anger at baseline and increasing anger over time, whereas anger decreased among those without clinical prolonged grief.
This finding is consistent with the conceptualization of anger and bitterness as manifestations of the intense emotional pain that may accompany prolonged grief .

It also aligns with findings among homicidally bereaved adults showing longitudinal associations between prolonged grief and anger, with prolonged grief more strongly predicting subsequent anger than the reverse direction .

Similarly, bereavement-related distress has been associated with externalizing symptoms among persistently delinquent adolescents, even after accounting for PTSD, maltreatment, and other clinical factors .
Extending this literature, our findings demonstrate that clinical prolonged grief is prospectively associated with increased anger among parentally bereaved youth.
Several mechanisms may contribute to the association between prolonged grief and anger.
According to the integrative risk-factor framework, grief adaptation is shaped by pre-loss vulnerabilities, experiences surrounding the death, and post-loss individual and family processes .
Beliefs that the death could have been prevented, perceived accountability, self-blame, and exposure to an unexpected or violent death have been associated with more severe grief symptoms .
Such beliefs may sustain feelings of injustice, blame, frustration, and bitterness, thereby interfering with the integration of the loss and contributing to increasing anger.

Disruptions in surviving-caregiver functioning, family cohesion, social support, and the caregiver-child relationship following parental death may further limit opportunities for youth to process the loss and regulate these emotions.

Importantly, prolonged grief was not associated with physical aggression, indicating that prolonged grief does not necessarily translate into overt aggressive or violent behavior.
Anger represents the affective component of aggression, whereas physical aggression reflects its behavioral expression and may be shaped by additional individual and situational factors .

Given that our study focused on a community-based sample, youth experiencing prolonged grief may express their distress primarily through anger without engaging in overt physical aggression, which may require the presence of additional vulnerabilities.

Furthermore, our previous study examined the effects of bereavement on a broad range of health-risk behaviors rather than the specific effects of prolonged grief, whereas another study examined grief-related distress among persistently delinquent youth who were already at elevated risk for externalizing behavior.
Thus, differences between these findings may reflect variation in sample characteristics, risk for behavioral disorders, and the specificity of the outcomes examined.

Our findings suggest that within a community-based sample of bereaved youth, prolonged grief may be more directly related to the emotional experience of anger than to its behavioral expression through physical aggression.

We also found that physical aggression increased more steeply among participants bereaved by sudden natural death than among those bereaved by suicide, whereas changes in physical aggression over time following accidental death did not differ significantly from that following natural death.

This finding was unexpected given prior studies reporting greater anger and behavioral problems following parental suicide and greater risks of violent criminality following external, unnatural, or suicidal parental deaths .

However, this finding partially aligns a previous study , who found that violent criminality was more strongly associated with unnatural parental deaths other than suicide than with parental suicide, indicating that suicide bereavement may not necessarily pose the greatest risk for violent criminality.

This study suggested that, in some cases, parental suicide may be preceded by recognizable psychiatric difficulties, allowing families or services to anticipate the possibility of a suicide death and initiate protective support .

In addition, it is possible that families bereaved by suicide had experienced greater pre-loss psychiatric morbidity, family disruption, and reduced parental involvement, whereas sudden natural death may have represented a more profound disruption to previously stable family relationships, as indicated in a previous study.
Our results should be interpreted while considering several limitations.
This is one of the few community studies with a 7-year follow-up period that examined multiple domains of highly relevant risk factors with relatively good retention.
An important limitation concerns the representativeness of our sample and the characteristics of those retained.

Participants who remained in the study were predominantly White, and although not significant after correcting for multiple comparisons, their surviving parents tended to have higher functionality and lower prolonged grief symptoms.
This pattern may bias our findings and limit generalizability to more clinically severe and ethnically diverse populations.
In addition, we included both adolescents and young adults in our study, known to differ developmentally.
Different developmental forces may influence outcomes for youth who lose a parent in childhood compared with those who experience this loss closer to young adulthood .

Even though age was not significantly associated with prolonged grief symptoms in our study, our sample size prevented us from examining age as a moderator and from determining whether outcomes differed between adolescents and young adults.

Taken together, this community-based longitudinal study extends prior research by distinguishing the emotional experience of anger from overt physical aggression and examining their trajectories across seven years following sudden parental death.
Clinical prolonged grief, rather than bereavement alone, was associated with higher and increasing anger over time.

The type of parental death, rather than bereavement or prolonged grief, was associated with increases in physical aggression over time, with steeper increases following sudden natural death than suicide.

Those findings highlight the potential importance of strengthening family functioning and relationships after sudden parental deaths and the importance of assessing prolonged grief and anger among bereaved youth.
